name: Magnetic rotation of polarization
summary: Faraday found in 1845 that a magnetic field twists the plane of polarized light passing through heavy glass, the first evidence that magnetism acts on light.
description: Polarized light traversing Faraday’s heavy glass along a magnetic field changed its plane of polarization; reversing the magnetic poles reversed the rotation.
tier_reason: The scoped record is a particular configuration, local witness, trial or material application. Dependence across fields or generations on THIS referent is not established; do not inherit the importance of its broader missing family.

impact.note: One experiment gave physicists the first evidence that magnetism acts on light, and magneto-optics and part of field theory grew from it.

why: Faraday believed light, electricity and magnetism were related, and his dense lead glass from the 1820s optical-glass work gave him a suitable test medium.

market.note: Commercial availability is not a milestone of a scientific knowledge result.

date.label: by 1845
date.basis: The paper was received on 6 November 1845 and describes the inquiry as recently resumed; the inspected passage establishes an observation by 1845, not its precise experimental date.

events.statement: Polarized light traversing Faraday’s heavy glass along a magnetic field changed its plane of polarization; reversing the magnetic poles reversed the rotation.
events.caveats: The material was his successful experimental medium, not a universal requirement for the effect; the paper also reports other substances and permanent magnets. This is distinct from mechanical electromagnetic rotation in 1821.

evidence.supports: 1845 communication, apparatus, named glass, extinction test and reversal.

date.label: by 27 October 1864
date.basis: Maxwell’s paper, received 27 October 1864, uses Faraday’s observed effect; the date of Maxwell’s first use is not established.

events.statement: By 27 October 1864 Maxwell had used Faraday’s magnetic rotation as an observational indication in his field-theory argument.
events.population: James Clerk Maxwell in electromagnetic-theory research
events.caveats: This is a narrowly documented intellectual use by Maxwell; it is neither universal acceptance nor evidence that Faraday’s effect uniquely derived Maxwell’s theory. The physical location of Maxwell’s relevant work is not established by the inspected passage.

evidence.supports: Maxwell invokes Faraday’s rotation and credits W. Thomson for an interpretation involving motion.

links.statement: Faraday explicitly identifies the heavy optical glass from his earlier research as the material with which he first obtained magnetic rotation of polarized light.
links.alternatives: The same paper reports the effect in other transparent substances and with permanent magnets.
links.caveats: The exact production date of the 1845 specimen is unspecified; identity is by composition and Faraday’s own explicit backward reference.
links.timing: The glass preparation was reported in 1829; its documented magneto-optical use is in 1845.

evidence.supports: Direct identification of the prior glass and its use in the observed rotation.
